```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = nzchar(params$data.file), message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.path = "pf_cacoa_harmony_files/figure-gfm/", dpi = 90)
```

This notebook is a companion of `pf_cacoa.Rmd`. The main notebook runs on the Conos object of the Cacoa preprint, whose
graph is the mutual-nearest-neighbor alignment of the 22 lungs, and its cluster-free density map calls no cell at
FDR 10 % although the composition analysis calls the basal cells, the `SCGB3A2+` cells, the aberrant basaloid
`KRT5-/KRT17+` cells and the AT1 cells clearly. `pf_density_diagnosis.md` traces that to the alignment: the Conos
graph consists almost entirely of cross-sample edges, and a population that a sample lacks is matched to that sample's
closest other population, so the heat kernel of the density map leaks out of the IPF-emergent populations (an AT1
cell's kernel keeps a fifth of its mass on AT1 cells). Here the same cells, counts and annotation are placed on a kNN
graph of a Harmony embedding (`prepare_pf_harmony.R`: 2,000 variable genes, 50 PCs, Harmony by sample, 30 nearest
neighbors on 30 Harmony dimensions, UMAP on the same), and only the parts of the analysis that depend on the graph are
rerun: the cluster-free density and expression-shift maps. The cell-type-level analyses (composition, expression shifts,
differential expression) use the counts and the annotation alone and are the same as in the main notebook.

```{r libs}
library(cacoa)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
```

## Load data

```{r load}
seu <- readRDS(params$data.file)
lib.meta <- readr::read_csv(params$lib.meta, show_col_types = FALSE, na = c("", "NA", "Unknown")) %>%
  filter(Diagnosis %in% c("Control", "IPF"))
cell.meta <- read.csv(params$cell.meta, row.names = 1) %>% filter(Diagnosis %in% c("Control", "IPF"))
sample.meta <- lib.meta %>%
  group_by(Sample_Name) %>%
  summarise(Diagnosis = first(Diagnosis), Processing_site = first(Processing_site), Chemistry = first(Chemistry),
            Gender = first(Gender), Age = as.integer(first(Age)), Tobacco = first(Tobacco), Flowcell_ID = first(Flowcell_ID),
            seq.saturation = mean(readr::parse_number(Sequencing_Saturation))) %>%
  left_join(cell.meta %>% group_by(Sample_Name) %>%
              summarise(Sample_Source = first(Sample_Source), n.cells = n(), median.umi = median(nCount_RNA), percent.mt = median(percent.mt)),
            by = "Sample_Name") %>%
  tibble::column_to_rownames("Sample_Name")
samples <- sort(unique(seu$sample))
sample.meta <- sample.meta[samples, c("Diagnosis", "Processing_site", "Sample_Source", "Chemistry", "Gender", "Age", "Tobacco",
                                     "Flowcell_ID", "n.cells", "median.umi", "percent.mt", "seq.saturation")]
table(sample.meta$Diagnosis)
```

```{r construct, message=TRUE}
cao <- Cacoa$new(seu, sample.metadata = sample.meta, sample.per.cell = factor(seu$sample), cell.groups = factor(seu$celltype),
                 embedding = seu@reductions$umap@cell.embeddings, graph.name = "RNA_nn", data.layer = "data", n.cores = params$n.cores)
```

```{r options}
cao$setOptions(n.permutations = 499, seed = 1)
cao$plot.params <- list(size = 0.1, alpha = 0.1, font.size = c(2, 3))
cao$sample.groups.palette <- c(Control = "#4575b4", IPF = "#d73027")
```

The graph used is Seurat's kNN graph on the Harmony embedding (`RNA_nn`, symmetrized; the shared-neighbor graph `RNA_snn`
has two components). It differs from the Conos graph in one respect that matters for the maps: 31 % of its edge weight
joins cells of the same sample (2 % on the Conos graph), so a cell whose population is absent from the other samples is
linked to its own sample's cells of that population instead of to other populations elsewhere.

```{r embedding, fig.width=11, fig.height=5}
cowplot::plot_grid(cao$plotEmbedding(color.by = "cell.groups", title = "cell type"),
                   cao$plotEmbedding(color.by = "Diagnosis", title = "diagnosis", mark.groups = FALSE, show.legend = TRUE), ncol = 2)
```

```{r set-model}
cao$setModel(~ Diagnosis, test = "Diagnosis")
```

## Cluster-free density shifts

The same map as in the main notebook: the default diffusion neighborhoods (`scale = "auto"`, a scan over 1, 3 and 5 %
of the cells), each sample's kernel density tested on the log scale with the model, cells adjusted by the pooled
permutation false-discovery rate.

```{r density, fig.width=15, fig.height=4.8, message=TRUE}
cao$estimateCellDensity(method = "graph")
cao$estimateDiffCellDensity()
cowplot::plot_grid(cao$plotEmbedding(color.by = "cell.groups", title = "cell type"),
                   cao$plotDiffCellDensity(what = "effect", title = "density change (log2 FC)", outline = TRUE),
                   cao$plotDiffCellDensity(title = "adjusted z", outline = TRUE), ncol = 3)
```

On this graph the scan picks the 1 % scale (neighborhoods of about 870 cells) and calls 11,452 cells (13 %) at
FDR 10 %, where the Conos graph called none. The calls are the populations the composition analysis names: 96 % of the
basal cells (log2 fold change 1.9), 79 % of the `KRT5-/KRT17+` cells (1.4), 59 % of the `SCGB3A2+` cells (1.0), 84-86 %
of the `MUC5B+`, `SCGB3A2+ SCGB1A1+` and cDC populations (1.1-1.2), and six types pass the per-type test (basal and cDCs
0.002, `KRT5-/KRT17+` and `SCGB3A2+ SCGB1A1+` 0.004, `MUC5B+` and `SCGB3A2+` 0.008; adjusted 0.03-0.04). The losses show
in the effect (AT1 -0.8, NK cells -0.9, AT2 -0.6, monocytes -0.3) but are not called at this scale: the AT1 cells are 568
cells, fewer than a neighborhood holds, and their neighbors, the transitional AT2 and `SCGB3A2+` cells, go the other way
(6 % of the AT1 cells called, per-type p 0.056). The effects stay well below the compositional fold changes (basal 4.2,
`KRT5-/KRT17+` 4.2, AT1 -4.1): a neighborhood of 870 cells around a cell of a 400-cell population is mostly other cells,
and the tail of the kernel adds more.

The kNN neighborhoods of the graph itself (`scale = NULL`: the stored units of `estimateCellDensity()`, about 220 cells
each) are the other neighborhood definition available; they are one hop wide, so they cannot leak the way a kernel can.

```{r density-knn, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.8, message=TRUE}
cao$estimateCellDensity(method = "graph", name = "cell.density.knn")
cao$estimateDiffCellDensity(name = "cell.density.knn", scale = NULL)
cowplot::plot_grid(cao$plotDiffCellDensity(name = "cell.density.knn", what = "effect", title = "kNN units: density change (log2 FC)", outline = TRUE),
                   cao$plotDiffCellDensity(name = "cell.density.knn", title = "kNN units: adjusted z", outline = TRUE), ncol = 2)
```

The kNN units resolve the small populations better: 25,886 cells (29 %) at FDR 10 %, with the same leading types
(basal 96 % at log2 2.8, `KRT5-/KRT17+` 89 % at 2.3, `MUC5B+` 76 %, cDCs 81 %, `SCGB3A2+` 55 %) and now the losses as
well: 51 % of the AT1 cells (-1.5; per-type p 0.03), 24 % of the AT2 cells (-1.5), and parts of the macrophage (41 %,
-0.7) and endothelial (41 %, -0.8) populations, which the composition does not call as types (fold changes -0.3 and
-0.2) but which the units see as local shifts within the types. The per-type test calls the same six types (adjusted p
0.037-0.052). On the Conos graph the kNN units called 4,599 cells and the kernel none (`pf_density_diagnosis.md`).

## Cluster-free expression shifts

```{r cluster-free-shifts, fig.width=13, fig.height=6, message=TRUE, warning=FALSE}
cao$estimateClusterFreeExpressionShifts(n.permutations = 499)
cao$plotClusterFreeExpressionShifts(adjusted = TRUE, font.size = c(2, 3), outline = TRUE)
```

The expression-shift map depends much less on the graph: its neighborhoods are large (the scan picks the 3 % scale,
as on the Conos graph: 125 neighborhoods of about 2,100 cells here, 300 of about 2,700 there) and the test is on
expression, which the alignment does not change. 87 % of the cells pass FDR 5 % (86 % on the Conos graph) and 26 of the
31 types are significant (25 there; the B cells and the proliferating T cells are significant here and not there, the
pDCs the other way round). The ranking of the strongest shifts differs: here the `MUC5AC+ High` and `MUC5B+` secretory
cells lead (median 3.0 and 2.7), followed by `SCGB3A2+` and `SCGB3A2+ SCGB1A1+` (2.3), the transitional AT2 cells (2.1),
AT1 and `KRT5-/KRT17+` (2.0) and the endothelial cells (1.8), while the basal cells, among the strongest on the Conos
graph (2.6), have a median of 1.6. The T and NK cells are not shifted (medians 1.14 and 1.07, under 1 % of their cells
called), nor are the plasma cells (18 %), the pDCs (21 %) and the mast cells (3 %); the proliferating macrophages are
significant (97 % of their cells called), and the proliferating T cells and the ciliated cells have the smallest
significant shifts (1.20 and 1.21; 89 % and 82 % of their cells called).

```{r cluster-free-summary, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.5}
cao$estimateClusterFreeSummary("cell.density")
cao$estimateClusterFreeSummary("cluster.free.expr.shifts")
cowplot::plot_grid(cao$plotClusterFreeSummary("cell.density"), cao$plotClusterFreeSummary("cluster.free.expr.shifts"), ncol = 2)
```

Per type, six populations change in density on this graph (the basal, `KRT5-/KRT17+`, `SCGB3A2+`, `SCGB3A2+ SCGB1A1+`,
`MUC5B+` and cDC populations, 45-93 % of their cells called at FDR 5 %) and 26 of 31 in expression. Together with
`pf_density_diagnosis.md` this settles the null density map of the main notebook: the statistic finds the compositional
changes once the neighborhoods stay within the populations, and on the Conos alignment of this cohort, where populations
present in only part of the lungs are matched to other populations in the lungs lacking them, they do not.
